cases.input:
What are all the books and papers this draft leans on? I want to make sure I credit everything.

"When I started thinking about why security programs stall, I kept coming back to Donella Meadows' Thinking in Systems, especially her chapter on leverage points. Most teams push on parameters when the real lever is the goal of the system. I also borrowed the idea of normal accidents from Charles Perrow's book of the same name, and a little from Sidney Dekker's The Field Guide to Understanding Human Error. There's a 2019 paper from the fictional Halvorsen Institute, 'Alert Fatigue and the Economics of Triage,' that gave me the numbers on analyst burnout. And honestly, the whole framing owes a debt to Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings, because the Ring is just a metaphor for a single shared credential nobody wants to give up. Last thing: I keep quoting Aesop's fable of the scorpion and the frog when I explain insider risk."
cases.expects: A bulleted list of every book, paper, story and fable the draft actually cites (Meadows, Perrow, Dekker, the Halvorsen paper, Tolkien, Aesop), one short bullet each of no more than 16 words with title and author where given. Nothing is invented or added from outside the passage, and the ideas the essay discusses are not listed as references.

cases.input:
Run extract references on this transcript excerpt:

"...so the thing I tell people building agents is go read The Mythical Man-Month, because Brooks already told us adding people to a late project makes it later, and the same thing is true of adding agents. Then there's that Sutton essay, The Bitter Lesson, which I think is the most important short piece in AI. Someone in the chat asked about the Anthropic paper on agentic misalignment, and yeah, read that too, though I only skimmed it. My friend at example.com keeps recommending a podcast called Signal Drift, I haven't listened yet. For fiction, Neuromancer and also Snow Crash, because both got the shape of the internet weirdly right. Oh and the Orwell, Nineteen Eighty-Four, obviously, for anyone talking about surveillance. We should also do a video on the CIS Controls at some point, but that's a framework, not something I've read cover to cover."
cases.expects: A bulleted list of the real sources mentioned (Mythical Man-Month, The Bitter Lesson, the agentic misalignment paper, Signal Drift, Neuromancer, Snow Crash, Nineteen Eighty-Four, and arguably the CIS Controls), each bullet at most 16 words with authors where stated. It stays within the up-to-20 cap, invents no authors or details the speaker did not give, and does not pad the list with non-sources.
